Theme

School & learning

figurative adjective and adverb

also figuratively, metaphorical, metaphorically, in a figurative sense

classical

Cic. Or. 27.92: trānslāta dīcō … quae per similitūdinem ab aliā rē … trānsferuntur (Lewis & Short s.v. trānsferō)
Quint. 8.3.24: cum sint autem verba propria, ficta, trānslāta
Traupman 314

trānslātus, trānslāta, trānslātum

figurative, used in a transferred sense (of a word)

A word carried over to another sense by likeness, verbum trānslātum: Cicero’s and Quintilian’s term, against proprium. A metaphor is trānslātiō (Cic. de Or. 3.38.156, Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • figūrātē — figuratively

    adverb · also used · post-classical · Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2.6 (Lewis & Short s.v. figūrō); Traupman 239, 246

    Traupman’s adverb (propriē an figūrātē?, 239). Quintilian’s figūrātus is said of speech made with figures of speech (9.1.13), not quite of a word used in a transferred sense.

  • trānslātīvus, trānslātīva, trānslātīvum — figurative

    also used · late Latin · Isid. 17.6.23 (Lewis & Short, for the adverb trānslātīvē); Traupman 246

    In Cicero and Quintilian a term of rhetoric for a plea that moves a case to another court; the sense “metaphorical” is Isidore’s, for the adverb.

  • per trānslātiōnem, trānslātīs verbīs — figuratively

    also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 3.37.149: words quae trānsferuntur (Lewis & Short s.v. trānsferō); Traupman 315

    Adverbial phrases for “figuratively”: by metaphor, in transferred words.

Examples

  • cum verbum aliquod altius trānsfertur

    when some word is carried over more boldlyCic. Or. 25.82 (Lewis & Short s.v. trānsferō)

  • Quārē? — Quia prō «bellō» pōnitur.

    Why? — Because it is used for “war”.Traupman 239

See also literal, mean, word.
